definition: The official name of a fiber class, such as polyester, nylon or elastane, that fiber-content labels in regulated markets must use in place of, or alongside, any trademark.
explanation: Labeling laws identify fibers by class, not by brand. For manufactured fibers, each generic name is tied to a written definition of chemical composition, typically a minimum proportion of a particular repeat unit in the polymer chain. In the United States, 16 CFR 303.7 sets out the generic names and definitions used under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and incorporates the names in ISO 2076. In the European Union, the permitted names are listed in Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Natural fibers are named by their common names, such as cotton or silk, under each jurisdiction's rules.
example: A swimsuit hangtag reads '80% nylon, 20% spandex' and prints a stretch-fiber trademark in smaller type nearby. The generic names carry the regulated information: which polymer classes are present and in what proportions by weight. The trademark only signals a producer's product line. A student comparing two swimsuits should compare generic names and percentages first, then treat any trademark as a separate, producer-specific statement.
caution: A generic name describes chemistry, not source, quality or impact. 'Polyester' covers virgin and recycled material alike, 'viscose' or 'rayon' says nothing about where the pulp was harvested, and 'bamboo' names a plant, not a generic name for a regenerated cellulose fiber made from it. Vocabulary also differs between jurisdictions, so 'spandex' on a US label and 'elastane' on an EU label can describe the same fiber class.
deeper: Generic definitions are written as compositional thresholds. The US rule defines polyester, for example, by the weight proportion of the chain formed from an ester of a substituted aromatic carboxylic acid, and spandex by the proportion formed from segmented polyurethane. A fiber that meets no existing definition cannot simply adopt a nearby name; a manufacturer can petition the Federal Trade Commission to establish a new one, and PLA (polylactic acid) is among the names now defined in the section. By incorporating ISO 2076:2013, the sixth edition dated 15 November 2013, Section 303.7 lets producers selling in several countries use internationally agreed names. Enforcement ultimately relies on laboratory identification, such as microscopy, solubility behavior and infrared spectroscopy, to check that a fiber matches the definition its label claims.
origins: The legal requirement comes from the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act, approved on 2 September 1958, which directed the Federal Trade Commission to establish generic names for manufactured fibers as new synthetic and regenerated fibers multiplied. The FTC has revised the list over time; it amended Part 303 in a final rule published in February 2020, and the current section incorporates the 2013 edition of ISO 2076. The European list evolved through earlier textile-name directives before being consolidated into Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011.

definition: The temperature range over which the disordered (amorphous) regions of a polymer change from a rigid, glassy state to a softer, rubbery state in which chain segments can move.
explanation: Below its glass transition, a polymer's disordered chain segments are effectively frozen and the material is stiff. Above it, segments gain enough thermal energy to rotate and slide, so the amorphous regions soften while crystalline regions stay intact until the melting point. For synthetic fibers this matters in drawing, heat setting, texturing, dyeing and ironing: a shape imposed above the glass transition and then cooled below it is locked in. Absorbed water acts as a plasticizer in hydrophilic polymers such as nylon and wool, lowering the effective transition temperature, which is why damp fabrics crease and set more easily.
example: A student irons two polyester swatches, one at a temperature below the fiber's glass transition and one well above it but far below melting. Only the hotter swatch keeps a sharp pleat after cooling. Repeating the test with a nylon swatch that has been dampened shows that moisture also lowers the temperature at which the fabric can be reshaped.
caution: The glass transition is not melting and is not a single sharp point. Reported values depend on method and conditions: a review of melt-spun fibers gives about 75 C for PET, while a dynamic mechanical study of electrospun PET membranes reported roughly 90 to 110 C. Heating rate, crystallinity, orientation and moisture also shift results, so a Tg figure alone does not predict safe ironing or dyeing temperatures.
deeper: Below Tg the amorphous chains are locked; above it, segmental motion opens free volume, raising extensibility and letting small molecules such as dyes diffuse. PET's Tg of roughly 75 C lets as-spun PET remain a stable, supercooled melt, and slow-crystallizing polymers such as PET are drawn slightly above Tg; disperse dyeing of polyester is run well above Tg, for example at 130 C under pressure. Water is a strong plasticizer: in a study of polyamide 6,6, water-saturated samples showed a DSC glass transition more than 80 degrees lower than dry ones. For wool, DSC data fitted with the Fox equation gave a dry Tg of about 174 C, falling as water content rises. Tg is measured by differential scanning calorimetry as a step in heat capacity or by dynamic mechanical analysis as a loss peak, and the two methods give different numbers.
origins: The name comes from inorganic glasses, which soften gradually over a temperature range instead of melting at one point; polymer scientists adopted it for the comparable softening of amorphous regions in plastics and fibers. Classic mixing rules remain in use: the Fox equation, developed to estimate the Tg of blends and plasticized polymers, is still applied to keratin fibers to model how absorbed water lowers Tg. In textiles the concept became central with melt-spun synthetics, whose drawing, texturing and heat setting are planned around it.
